case_analysis.focal_point: The legality of the Biden administration's student loan forgiveness program, specifically whether the Secretary of Education has the statutory authority to implement it under the HEROES Act and whether the challenging states have standing to sue.
case_analysis.legal_provision: The case concerns the Secretary of Education's authority to implement a 'universal suspension of both loan payments and interest on student loans,' an action taken under the Higher Education Relief Opportunities for Students (HEROES) Act of 2003.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The petitioners (Biden administration) argue that the Secretary of Education possesses the authority under the HEROES Act to implement the student loan forgiveness program in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, and that the respondent states lack standing to challenge the program.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The respondents (states, led by Nebraska) argue that the Secretary of Education exceeded statutory authority under the HEROES Act by enacting such a broad student loan forgiveness program, and that they have standing to challenge the program due to direct harm.
key_precedents: McNabb v. United States, 318 U.S. 332, 341 (1943) (mentioned in the context of the Court's supervisory authority, not the merits of the student loan program)

Our jurisdiction is limited to actual 'cases and controversies,' and without proper standing, this Court lacks the authority to address the merits, including the application of the Major Questions Doctrine articulated in *West Virginia v. EPA* by many of my colleagues. Resolving standing first is a fundamental principle of judicial minimalism and institutional legitimacy, preventing the Court from issuing advisory opinions on policy matters.
